title: Inside the browser: from DOM click to socket
intro: The browser scheduler runs JavaScript. Reflex’s event queue is an array inside that JavaScript, not another thread.

phases.title: React invokes the generated callback
phases.note: The browser delivers the interaction and React invokes the button callback. The next local phases describe a call chain, not separate browser tasks.
phases.payload:
DOM click → React callback(_e)
Call stack: generated onClick

phases.title: Build an application event
phases.note: The callback constructs a ReflexEvent. The native/React interaction object stays in the browser; only the required application arguments are selected.

phases.title: addEvents applies event actions
phases.note: Connection setup is requested when appropriate. applyEventActions handles configured preventDefault, stopPropagation, temporal, throttle, or debounce behavior. This button has none.

phases.title: Enqueue a Reflex event
phases.note: queueEvents appends to a module-level array and calls processEvent. This snapshot is transient; dispatch can begin immediately.

phases.title: Take the next event and attach routing
phases.note: With the socket connected, processEvent shifts the event. applyEvent chooses the socket path and fills router_data. The array is not a server-completion tracker.

phases.title: Emit the event
phases.note: socket.emit sends the event object. Awaiting local applyEvent does not await the Python handler or a final=true response.

phases.title: Python works; the click callback can finish
phases.note: Python processes the session event. The browser does not synchronously execute it. Other browser work can run after the JavaScript callback yields or returns.
phases.payload:
Python: increment() → count=1, doubled=2
Browser: original click callback no longer waiting

phases.title: Socket.IO invokes the incoming listener
phases.note: The receive callback is a new entry into frontend JavaScript. It receives a StateUpdate rather than resuming a blocked Python call.

phases.title: Dispatch into the substate reducer
phases.note: The listener validates substate names, dispatches deltas, updates configured storage, and handles returned frontend events. React receives the merged context values.

phases.title: React commits the updated UI
phases.note: React renders and commits the affected DOM; the browser paints when appropriate. No page recompilation happened.

title: From Python objects to a runnable browser app
intro: Follow the artifacts. UI declarations produce React modules; Python event handlers stay on the backend.

phases.title: Execute the page-building code
phases.note: Python calls component constructors. This creates objects describing the interface, not HTML in a browser.

phases.title: Build the component tree
phases.note: The actual button render dictionary contains a component name, properties, event expression, and child text.

phases.title: Resolve symbolic state references
phases.note: LabState.count in a page is an expression linked to a React state context. self.count in a backend handler is a Python value.

phases.title: Generate the React module
phases.note: The compiler emits imports, hooks, event callbacks, and component rendering code. This is an actual generated button excerpt.

phases.title: Generate contexts and initial data
phases.note: Initial public defaults and reducers become JavaScript. Compilation does not retrieve a future visitor’s saved session.

phases.title: Bundle the frontend for production

phases.title: Serve the SPA document and assets
phases.note: The browser receives HTML referencing runnable JavaScript modules. The inspector shows the actual generated production HTML, not a Socket.IO message.

phases.title: React renders; Python handles later events
phases.note: JavaScript executes React components and creates the DOM. A later click sends an event to Python; it does not recompile the app.
phases.payload:
HTML → JavaScript entry → React providers → route → DOM

Later: click → Socket.IO → Python increment() → delta → React

title: From an empty tab to live state
intro: HTTP brings the interface. The socket brings this session’s data. Follow both trips.

phases.title: Request the document
phases.note: The browser requests / from the frontend. This is HTTP, before the Reflex state socket exists.

phases.title: Load the interface
phases.note: The document references scripts and styles. The browser loads them and React initializes from compiled defaults. This diagram groups the separate asset requests.
phases.payload:
HTML document → script and CSS requests
React hydrateRoot(document, HydratedRouter)

phases.title: Initialize public defaults
phases.note: These values were compiled before this visitor connected. Empty router fields are placeholders, not missing runtime data.

phases.title: Establish the socket
phases.note: Socket.IO connects with a browser token. The backend associates its connection SID with that token. No user login is implied.

phases.title: Queue hydrate and page-load work
phases.note: initialEvents queues hydrate followed by on_load_internal. This app has no browser-storage values to insert between them.

phases.title: Receive the public snapshot
phases.note: Python sends current public state. This is a full synchronization; the payload below is an excerpt of the app substate.

phases.title: Run enter_home
phases.note: The on-load chain selects the Home handler, updates page and visits, then sets the root hydration flag.

phases.title: Render the synchronized page
phases.note: Page and hydration deltas reach React. Multiple actual frames are grouped here; no personalized HTML is sent by this event.

title: A click is a round trip, not new HTML
intro: Watch count stay at 0 in the browser until the server’s delta arrives.

phases.title: Click Add one
phases.note: The generated React callback builds a named event. It does not send count=1 or the complete DOM click object.

phases.title: Send the handler name
phases.note: Socket.IO sends this object. The established connection supplies the client token to the backend.

phases.title: Resolve the session and handler
phases.note: The processor selects this token’s LabState and enters its state modification context. This edge is an internal Python call, not a second network request.
phases.payload:
token → state manager → LabState
registered handler → increment()

phases.title: Mutate Python state
phases.note: count changes first. Its computed dependency doubled becomes 2. The private bookkeeping field changes too.

phases.title: Collect changed public fields
phases.note: Dirty tracking includes count and doubled. _handled stays backend-only. Unchanged name and page are omitted.

phases.title: Send the delta back
phases.note: The backend targets this client’s socket. The message contains values, not HTML or DOM instructions.

phases.title: Merge state and commit the DOM
phases.note: React receives the field updates. The reducer preserves omitted fields; React renders the new count and doubled values.

title: New page. Same counter. Same connection.
intro: This sequence begins after one click: count is 1 and the Home page has one visit.

phases.title: Follow the internal link
phases.note: The app link requests client-side navigation to /details. This is a local browser action.

phases.title: Select the Details component
phases.note: The location changes. Contexts preserve the current count; the navigation effect marks hydration false. Route code may load if it is not already available.
phases.payload:
location.pathname = "/details"
local is_hydrated = false
count remains 1

phases.title: Send on_load_internal
phases.note: The existing socket carries the new pathname and asPath. Normal internal navigation does not send a full hydrate event.

phases.title: Run enter_details
phases.note: The server updates router metadata, runs the page handler, and completes the on-load chain. Name and count do not change.

phases.title: Send route and page updates
phases.note: Several response frames are grouped here: router metadata, page/visits, and is_hydrated=true. The app-field excerpt shows no count reset.

phases.title: Finish the new page
phases.note: React merges the updates. Count is still 1. Refresh differs: it creates a new document/socket and performs full hydration again.
phases.payload:
Browser: count=1, page="Details", visits=2
Root: is_hydrated=true

title: Why initialState contains more than your counter
intro: Follow build-time placeholders as they become session-specific values. Only public fields cross to React.

phases.title: Ship the default state shape
phases.note: The compiler emits both the root and app substates. It knows Ada and count=0, but not this visitor’s headers, URL, token, or SID.

phases.title: Connect and identify this session
phases.note: The socket handshake supplies request headers and the browser’s token. The server associates the token with the connection SID.
phases.payload:
Host: localhost:8037
Origin: http://localhost:3037
Upgrade: websocket
Connection query: token=<CLIENT_TOKEN>

phases.title: Build the router context
phases.note: Connection metadata combines with event router_data. Headers describe the backend connection; router.url describes the frontend address.
phases.payload:
headers.host = "localhost:8037"
url.href = "http://localhost:3037/"
route_id = "/index"
session = {client_token: T, session_id: S}

phases.title: Hydrate public fields
phases.note: The session snapshot fills the placeholders. Private fields such as _handled and internal locks are excluded. The diagram uses short names for readability.

phases.title: Understand the empty internal substates
phases.note: An empty object means no public fields, not no behavior. These classes can register handlers and hold backend-only machinery.
